title: 10ish Cases of Really Bad Luck
summary: Josh and Chuck profile a list of people with notably bad luck (and a few whose bad-luck reputation is questionable). Covered: Ron Wayne, the third Apple co-founder who sold his 10% stake for a few thousand dollars twelve days after the 1976 partnership; Ann Hodges, struck by an 8.5-pound meteorite in Alabama in 1954; Pete Best, the Beatles drummer replaced just before they became famous; Melanie Martinez, whose houses were destroyed by hurricanes including Isaac in 2012; Jason Cairns, Lawrence and partner Jenny, present at three major terrorist attacks (9/11, the 2005 London bombings, and the 2008 Mumbai attacks); Antonio Meucci versus Alexander Graham Bell over the telephone; Costas Mitsotakas, who missed out on a shared Spanish El Gordo lottery win by his village; Richard Jewell, the security guard cleared after being named a suspect in the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Park bombing; and Frank Selak, the self-described luckiest man in the world, whose stories are unverified. The episode closes with a listener mail correcting an earlier episode on rape kits and the Golden State Killer.

segments.title: Opening banter and Chuck's traffic-ticket luck
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode about unlucky people and joke about Chuck avoiding speeding tickets by being humble with police.

segments.title: Ron Wayne and the Apple partnership
segments.summary: Ron Wayne, the third Apple co-founder, left the company after about twelve days, selling his ten percent stake for a few thousand dollars. He kept the first Apple contract, which later sold at auction for much more, and he has said he regrets the sale.

segments.title: Ann Hodges and the meteorite strike
segments.summary: Ann Hodges was reportedly hit by an 8.5-pound meteorite that came through her roof in Alabama, bounced off a radio, and hit her hip. A court fight with her landlord followed, and the rock's value later collapsed.

segments.title: Pete Best and the Beatles
segments.summary: Pete Best was the Beatles drummer during the Quarrymen and Hamburg period and was replaced just before the band's first recordings. Discussion covers the rumors about his looks, John Lennon's comments that he was a weak drummer, and Best's later royalties.

segments.title: Melanie Martinez and repeated hurricane losses
segments.summary: Melanie Martinez lost her house to hurricanes several times, including Betsy, Katrina, and Isaac. She was on a reality show makeover just before Isaac destroyed the house, and she and her family were trapped in the attic before being rescued.

segments.title: Survivor of three terrorist attacks
segments.summary: Jason Cairns Lawrence and his partner Jenny were present at three major terrorist attacks: New York on 9/11, London in July 2005, and Mumbai in 2008.

segments.title: Antonio Meucci versus Alexander Graham Bell
segments.summary: Antonio Meucci, an Italian inventor, filed a preliminary patent for a telephone-like device (the teletrophone) years before Bell. Meucci could not afford to renew it, Bell obtained his patent in 1876, and Meucci's lawsuit ended with his death. A 2002 House resolution recognized Meucci. Elisha Gray is also named as a rival claimant.

segments.title: Costas Mitsotakas and the El Gordo lottery
segments.summary: A Spanish village pooled money to buy El Gordo Christmas lottery tickets and won, but Costas Mitsotakas did not buy in because he was not visited by the fundraisers. He later made a documentary about the village and sold his property.

segments.title: Richard Jewell and the 1996 Olympic Park bombing
segments.summary: Security guard Richard Jewell spotted a suspicious backpack at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Park and helped clear the area before the pipe bomb exploded. He was then named a suspect, and was cleared in October; the real bomber was Eric Rudolph.

segments.title: Frank Selak and the unverified 'luckiest man' claims
segments.summary: Frank Selak was called the luckiest man in the world after telling stories of surviving seven brushes with death, which were first printed after a lottery win. A commenter claiming to be his son said the stories were made up, and the hosts note none have been independently verified.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Golden State Killer and rape kits
segments.summary: Listener Jessica Breslin corrects an earlier episode: the Golden State Killer's DNA was linked to his crimes in the 1990s but had no suspect to compare to until familial DNA searching in 2018.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and give contact information.
